Now I can see the pattern from the examples! Let me analyze them:

For FGI (Functional Group Interconversion):
1. `CCNc1nccc2c1c(C(N)=O)nn2-c1cccc(C#C[C@]2(O)CCN(C)C2=O)c1` → `CCNc1nccc2c1c(C(=O)OC)nn2-c1cccc(C#C[C@]2(O)CCN(C)C2=O)c1.N`
   - The amide C(N)=O is converted to ester C(=O)OC, and N is released
   
2. `CC(C)(C)c1cc(C=NO)c(O)c(-c2ccc(C(F)(F)F)nc2)c1` → `CC(C)(C)c1cc(C=O)c(O)c(-c2ccc(C(F)(F)F)nc2)c1.NO`
   - The oxime C=NO is converted to aldehyde C=O, and NO is released
   
3. `O=C1C(c2ccc(Br)cc2O)c2ccccc2N1C(c1ccccc1)c1ccccc1` → `O=C1N(C(c2ccccc2)c2ccccc2C1(O)c1ccc(Br)cc1O`
   - This one seems to be converting something... let me look more carefully
   - Actually this looks like it's converting a lactam/lactone situation
   
4. `CC[C@@]1(O)CC[C@@]2(Cc3ccccc3)c3ccc(C(=O)Nc4cccnc4C)cc3COC[C@H]2C1` → `CC[C@@]1(O)CC[C@@]2(Cc3ccccc3)c3ccc(C(=O)Nc4cccnc4C)cc3COC(O)[C@H]2C1`
   - The acetal/ether group gets hydrolyzed back to an alcohol, with the other fragment being lost

5. `C[C@H]1C[C@@H](c2ccncc2NC(=O)c2ccc(F)c(-c3c(F)cccc3F)n2)C[C@@H](NC(=O)OC(C)(C)C)[C@H]1N` → `C[C@H]1C[C@@H](c2ccncc2NC(=O)c2ccc(F)c(-c3c(F)cccc3F)n2)C[C@@H](NC(=O)OC(C)(C)C)[C@H]1N=[N+]=[N-]`
   - The primary amine transforms into a diazonium species

6. `COc1cccc(Nc2c(C(N)=O)cnc3c(C)cc(S(=O)(=O)c4cccc(C(=O)Nc5ccc(-c6ccc(C=O)cc6)cc5)c4)cc23)c1` → `COc1cccc(Nc2c(C(N)=O)cnc3c(C)cc(S(=O)(=O)c4cccc(C(=O)Nc5ccc(-c6ccc(CO)cc6)cc5)c4)cc23)c1`
   - An aldehyde group reduces to a primary alcohol

The pattern emerging is that FGI reactions involve swapping functional groups while releasing small molecules—esters convert to amides with alcohol byproducts, oximes become carbonyls with nitrogen oxide, acetals yield alcohols, and amines transform into diazonium compounds.
